correctness.rationale: Absolute deterministic threshold-two closure is characterized by two-neighbor forts: a seed set fails iff its complement contains a nonempty subset each of whose vertices has ≤1 neighbor outside. Explicit minimal forts of theta(2,2,3) and bridge-connected two triangles give full contagious-set vectors (0,0,0,10,14,6,1) and (0,0,0,12,13,6,1). Uniform k=3 ranking 10/20<12/20, k=4 ranking14/15>13/15. Independent complete bitmask enumeration visits all connected labeled graphs on n≤6 (1,1,4,38,728,26704), all 2^n seeds, all degree-sequence matched profile pairs; the sole reversing pair at n=6 is those profiles, occurring in 180 and 90 labeled graphs, equal to permutation orbit counts 6!/4 and 6!/8. Exact binomial summation yields independent-seed difference p³(1-p)²(3p−2), so the single interior crossover is 2/3. A six-vertex connected pair has seven edges, making two-seed full activation impossible via edge-count 2(6−2)=8.
residual_risks: Classification is genuinely exhaustive only through n=6; no claim about uniqueness for larger graphs.

value.rationale: Same-degree networks can reverse their chances of full adoption solely because the seed budget moves from three to four, and six is the uniquely sharp first order. This exact, fully classified structural counterexample shows degree statistics alone do not order a natural nonlinear diffusion success probability; the complete seed profiles and Bernoulli crossover at 2/3 are useful benchmarks for small network contagion design and analytic fort arguments.
residual_risks: Results concern deterministic irreversible threshold two and random initial seeds, not probabilistic transmission or real-world adoption forecasts.

limitations: No claim for n≥7 uniqueness or for fractional/heterogeneous activation thresholds.
